lead: Lagrange's linear equation is a first-order PDE of the form P p + Q q = R. Here z is the unknown surface, p = ∂z/∂x, q = ∂z/∂y, and P, Q, R are functions of x, y, z. The method turns the PDE into two ordinary first integrals along characteristic curves. Two independent integrals u = c₁, v = c₂ give the general solution φ(u, v) = 0. Engineers meet such equations when a surface must satisfy a slope condition everywhere, for example in geometry, streamline surfaces and simple conservation models.
prereq: You need 4.1 for p and q, and exact differentials from Unit 1.

sections.h3: The equation and its auxiliary system

blocks.text: Write the PDE in standard form before doing anything else. It is called linear because P, Q and R do not contain p or q. They may contain x, y and z in any way. A solution is a surface z = f(x, y) whose partial derivatives satisfy the equation at every point of a region.

blocks.where: P, Q, R are given functions of x, y, z; z is the unknown function of x and y; p = ∂z/∂x; q = ∂z/∂y.

blocks.text: Lagrange's idea is to move along special curves on the solution surface. Along such a curve, x, y and z all change together. The PDE becomes a system of ordinary differential equations. These are the auxiliary equations.

items: Identify P, Q and R after moving every term to one side.
Write the auxiliary equations dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R.
Find two independent first integrals u = c₁ and v = c₂.
Write the general solution as φ(u, v) = 0, or as u = f(v).

blocks.text: Introduce a parameter t along a characteristic curve. Then dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R = dt gives dx = P dt, dy = Q dt and dz = R dt. Choose multipliers l, m, n such that lP + mQ + nR = 0. Multiplying the three differentials and adding gives l dx + m dy + n dz = 0. If the left side is an exact differential dF, integrate it to get F = constant. That constant is one first integral.

Two first integrals u = c₁ and v = c₂ are independent when neither is a function of the other on the region. Equivalently, their gradients are not parallel there. One independent relation between u and v remains arbitrary. That is why a single first-order PDE has a whole family of solution surfaces, not one surface.

items: Common multiplier choices are 1, 1, 1 or x, y, z, but only when the sum condition holds.
A multiplier triple that gives a new constant is useful; one that repeats an old constant is not.
The general solution is φ(u, v) = 0 or u = f(v); φ and f are arbitrary functions.
A first-order PDE in two independent variables needs exactly two independent first integrals.

blocks.text: Each solution z = f(x, y) is an integral surface. The auxiliary equations give characteristic curves. Any characteristic curve that touches an integral surface lies wholly on that surface. Changing c₁ and c₂ selects different characteristic curves; the integral surface is woven from them. This picture explains why the general solution contains an arbitrary function: many surfaces can be built from the same family of curves.

Lagrange's method handles linear equations P p + Q q = R. Nonlinear first-order equations need Charpit's method. An initial curve selecting one surface is the Cauchy problem. Pfaffian equations appear in 4.6. Second-order PDEs start in Unit 5. Some syllabi call this topic Lagrange's linear PDE or the linear equation of first order.

figure.caption: The auxiliary ratios lead to two multiplier choices; each choice gives one constant, and together they fix the general solution.

spec.title: Lagrange example (y−z)p+(z−x)q=x−y
spec.aria: Flowchart shows the auxiliary ratios for the example and two multiplier choices that yield x+y+z=c₁ and x²+y²+z²=c₂.

examples.question: Solve (y − z)p + (z − x)q = x − y. Also evaluate the two first integrals at the point (x, y, z) = (1, 2, 3).
steps: Identify the coefficients: P = y − z, Q = z − x, R = x − y.
Write the auxiliary equations: dx/(y − z) = dy/(z − x) = dz/(x − y).
Take multipliers 1, 1, 1. Their sum with the denominators is (y − z) + (z − x) + (x − y) = 0.
Therefore dx + dy + dz = 0. Integrate: x + y + z = c₁.
Take multipliers x, y, z. Their sum is x(y − z) + y(z − x) + z(x − y) = xy − xz + yz − xy + xz − yz = 0.
Therefore x dx + y dy + z dz = 0. Integrate: x² + y² + z² = c₂, with the factor 2 absorbed into the constant.
Independence at (1, 2, 3): gradients are (1, 1, 1) and (2, 4, 6), which are not parallel, so u = 6 and v = 14 are independent there.
examples.answer: The general solution is φ(x + y + z, x² + y² + z²) = 0, and at (1, 2, 3) the first integrals are u = 6 and v = 14.
examples.check:
x = 1
y = 2
z = 3
u = x + y + z
v = x*x + y*y + z*z
print(u)
print(v)

traps: The denominators are P, Q, R, not p, q, r. Writing dx/p = dy/q = dz/R mixes the unknown derivatives with the coefficients and is wrong.
Two first integrals must be independent. u = x + y and v = 2x + 2y give only one constant, not a general solution.
Multipliers must make lP + mQ + nR = 0. Checking l p + m q + n R = 0 is meaningless because p and q are unknown.
Do not force z as the subject unless an initial condition or the question asks for it. The implicit form φ(u, v) = 0 is the standard answer.
Constants may be scaled: x² + y² + z² = c and (x² + y² + z²)/2 = c describe the same family. Do not count them as two independent integrals.

quiz.q: Write the auxiliary equations for P p + Q q = R.
Why must multipliers l, m, n satisfy lP + mQ + nR = 0?
quiz.a: Along a characteristic, dx = P dt, dy = Q dt and dz = R dt. Then l dx + m dy + n dz = (lP + mQ + nR) dt. Setting the sum to zero makes this differential vanish, so it can be integrated to a constant.

quiz.q: Solve x p + y q = z.
quiz.a: Auxiliary equations: dx/x = dy/y = dz/z. Integrate dx/x = dy/y to get y/x = c₁. Integrate dx/x = dz/z to get z/x = c₂. General solution: φ(y/x, z/x) = 0.

quiz.q: Find the general solution of p + q = 1.
quiz.a: Auxiliary equations: dx/1 = dy/1 = dz/1. Then dx − dy = 0 gives x − y = c₁, and dy − dz = 0 gives y − z = c₂. General solution: φ(x − y, y − z) = 0.

quiz.q: Why are u = x + y and v = 2x + 2y not acceptable as two first integrals?
quiz.a: Because v = 2u, so v is a function of u. The two constants are not independent. A first-order PDE in two independent variables needs two independent first integrals to carry an arbitrary function.
It is the graph z = f(x, y) of a solution of the PDE. Characteristic curves that meet it lie on it.

quiz.q: Check whether u = x − y and v = x + y are independent at (1, 0).
quiz.a: Gradients are (1, −1) and (1, 1). Their determinant is (1)(1) − (−1)(1) = 2, which is nonzero, so they are independent at (1, 0).

quiz.q: In (y − z)p + (z − x)q = x − y, why is it a bad idea to divide by y − z and solve for p?
quiz.a: Division fails on the plane y = z, which may contain part of the solution. It also hides the symmetric auxiliary system that gives both first integrals. The multiplier method avoids this loss of information.

beyond: Not for the exam. Lagrange's method is the prototype of the method of characteristics used in traffic-flow models, gas dynamics and Hamilton-Jacobi equations. In computational fluid dynamics, characteristic surfaces guide where boundary conditions must be set. Search next for 'method of characteristics conservation laws' and 'Lagrange-Charpit equations'.
